title: From reading to writing - Nature Biotechnology
gist: DNA writing is entering rapid innovation as enzymatic and cellular methods challenge decades-old phosphoramidite chemistry, but none yet delivers long, accurate DNA at biological scale; removing this bottleneck would accelerate AI-driven protein design, cell therapy and synthetic biology.

themes.theme: DNA writing as the field's persistent bottleneck

insights.claim: Writing DNA from scratch remains a bottleneck for biotechnology, especially the synthesis of long, complex sequences and libraries, even as reading and editing DNA have been transformed.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Whoever solves cheap, fast, accurate long-DNA writing unlocks a chokepoint that gates protein engineering, gene therapy and synthetic biology.
insights.quote: Yet writing DNA from scratch is still a bottleneck for biotechnology, especially the synthesis of long, complex sequences and libraries.

insights.claim: There are four major classes of DNA synthesis technology, each solving a different part of the writing process and each with limitations.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: No single winner yet exists, so the DNA-writing market is still contestable across chemistry, assembly, enzymatic and cellular approaches.

insights.claim: Phosphoramidite chemistry, the industry standard, can generate DNA oligos up to 200 nucleotides and its four-step workflow is essentially unchanged since the early 1980s, with error rates becoming limiting over hundreds of cycles.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: A 40-year-old chemistry capped at ~200 nt is the incumbent every new entrant must beat on length and error rate.
insights.quote: Phosphoramidite chemistry, the industry standard, can generate DNA oligo sequences up to 200 nucleotides in length, and the workflow is essentially unchanged since the early 1980s.

themes.theme: New assembly methods: Sidewinder and MOSAIC

insights.claim: The Sidewinder three-way-junction technique uses a third strand carrying fragment-order information that never becomes part of the finished product, working well on repetitive sequences that defeat overlap-based assembly.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Solving repetitive-sequence assembly expands what genes can be built, but assembly methods still can't fix errors in the chemically made oligos they use.

insights.claim: MOSAIC (Molecular Self-Assembly Induced Cloning) couples programmable in vitro self-assembly of overlapping oligos with in vivo cellular DNA nick-repair machinery to build functional plasmids, even from difficult-to-assemble sequences.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: MOSAIC advances assembly length and speed, but like Sidewinder it inherits the error rate of chemically synthesized starting oligos.

insights.claim: Ansa Biotechnologies uses terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) conjugated to a single nucleotide to directly synthesize DNA over 1,000 bases long without assembling shorter oligos, at a small error rate of about 1 error per 1,000 bases.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Template-free, sequence-agnostic enzymatic synthesis past 1 kb is the clearest challenger to phosphoramidite, and its ~10^-3 error rate is the number to beat.
insights.quote: Ansa Biotechnologies has shown that it can use TdT conjugated to a single nucleotide to directly synthesize DNA molecules over 1,000 bases long without assembling shorter oligos.

insights.claim: Camena Bioscience uses an optimized proprietary enzyme mix to build and assemble DNA fragments, but its specific enzymes are proprietary and its data are not yet published.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: An unpublished, closed enzymatic approach is a competitive wildcard whose real performance can't yet be benchmarked.

insights.claim: Retrons, bacterial elements that make single-stranded DNA in cells from an RNA template, could enable intracellular DNA writing but so far have only produced sequences tens of base pairs long, needing a longer-range polymerase, error correction and product recovery to scale.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: In-cell programmable DNA writing is the long-horizon prize but remains far from practical length and fidelity.

themes.theme: Commercial opportunity and the AI feedback loop

insights.claim: The best commercial opportunity is probably therapeutic DNA manufacturing that fully replaces phosphoramidite synthesis for CRISPR therapeutics, gene therapy and CAR-T engineering.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Positions the near-term revenue pool for DNA-writing startups as the therapeutics supply chain, not research reagents.
insights.quote: The best commercial opportunity is probably therapeutic DNA manufacturing — complete replacement of phosphoramidite synthesis for DNA used in CRISPR therapeutics, gene therapy, CAR-T engineering and more.

insights.claim: As AI accelerates experimental science and labs computationally design thousands of DNA constructs in hours, physically building and testing them is the slowest and most expensive step, making faster accurate DNA writing the rate-limiter for the AI protein-design loop.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: AI design demand grows the addressable market for DNA writing, and synthesis speed becomes the binding constraint on AI-driven biology.
insights.quote: As AI continues to accelerate the pace of experimental science, the need for DNA sequences will grow.

insights.claim: Companies report high accuracy for longer sequences but still take weeks to deliver DNA products, so reliability plus speed — not accuracy alone — will decide commercial success.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Turnaround time is the underrated competitive axis; a vendor that keeps accuracy while cutting weeks to days wins the market.
insights.quote: While companies report high accuracy rates for longer sequences, they still take too long to generate DNA products (weeks).

insights.claim: A DNA sequencing benchmark for reliability will be necessary because any new method must prove its technology against others on sequences of varied complexity and length to achieve commercial success.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Expect a CASP-style benchmark to emerge as the arbiter that separates real DNA-writing advances from marketing claims.
